expectedText:
CALIFORNIA 'SHINE THE LIGHT' LAW — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc. · https://www.acme.com

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes California's "Shine the Light" law, Civil Code § 1798.83, prepared with reference to Acme, Inc., which may direct questions about this sheet to privacy@acme.com or (415) 555-0100. Section 1798.83 gives a California customer the right to request information about what personal information a business has disclosed to third parties for the third parties' own direct marketing purposes, and requires a covered business to either respond to such requests or adopt a specified alternative opt-out (or opt-in) policy instead. This is a distinct, older statute from the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA/CPRA) and from the California Online Privacy Protection Act (CalOPPA), addressed in other documents; § 1798.83 became operative January 1, 2005 and was last amended effective January 1, 2006, well before the CCPA (2018/2020) or CalOPPA's current form, and it targets a narrower question — third-party direct-marketing disclosure specifically — rather than a business's general data-collection or data-sale practices. Complying with the CCPA or CalOPPA does not by itself satisfy, and is not required in order to trigger, this separate duty, which has its own conditions, its own required response, and its own alternative compliance path. This sheet is an informational record only. It does not itself determine that Acme, Inc. is a business covered by Civil Code § 1798.83, does not determine that any specific disclosure by Acme, Inc. was made to a third party for the third party's direct marketing purposes, does not determine which of the statute's two compliance paths applies to Acme, Inc. or satisfies either path, and does not respond to, or draft a response to, any actual customer request.

WHICH BUSINESSES ARE COVERED, AND THE SMALL-BUSINESS EXEMPTION
The statute's duty to respond to a customer's request is not owed by every business that handles personal information — it is conditioned on a specific combination of facts about an established customer relationship and a prior disclosure. Under Civil Code § 1798.83(a), the duty attaches "if a business has an established business relationship with a customer and has within the immediately preceding calendar year disclosed personal information that corresponds to any of the categories of personal information set forth in paragraph (6) of subdivision (e) to third parties, and if the business knows or reasonably should know that the third parties used the personal information for the third parties' direct marketing purposes." All three elements — an established business relationship, an actual disclosure of a statutorily listed category of personal information within the preceding calendar year, and the business's actual or constructive knowledge that the recipient used it for the recipient's own direct marketing purposes — are conditions of the trigger language itself, not independent alternative triggers. Separately, the statute carves out businesses below a fixed size, regardless of whether the trigger conditions above are otherwise met: under § 1798.83(c)(1), "A business with fewer than 20 full-time or part-time employees is exempt from the requirements of this section."

Effective January 1, 2006.)," meaning this is the version of the statute currently in force as of the date this clause was checked, and that it has not been amended since 2006. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine that the business identified in this document has an established business relationship with any customer, that it disclosed any listed category of personal information to a third party within the preceding calendar year, that it knew or reasonably should have known of the third party's direct marketing use, or that it has fewer than 20 full-time or part-time employees.

HOW A CUSTOMER MAKES A REQUEST, AND THE BUSINESS'S DUTY TO DESIGNATE A CHANNEL
The statute specifies both how a customer may submit a request and a business's own corresponding duty to designate where such requests should be sent. As to the customer's request, § 1798.83(a) provides that a covered business's duty runs "after the receipt of a written or electronic mail request, or, if the business chooses to receive requests by toll-free telephone or facsimile numbers, a telephone or facsimile request from the customer" — meaning a customer may always request by mail or email, and may additionally request by toll-free phone or fax only if the business has elected to accept requests through those channels. As to the business's own duty, § 1798.83(b)(1) requires that "A business required to comply with this section shall designate a mailing address, electronic mail address, or, if the business chooses to receive requests by telephone or facsimile, a toll-free telephone or facsimile number, to which customers may deliver requests pursuant to subdivision (a)." The same paragraph goes on to require the business to take at least one of several further steps to make that designated channel known — including notifying customer-facing employees of it, or adding a "Your Privacy Rights" link to the business's website — which this clause does not quote in full.

WHAT THE RESPONSE MUST CONTAIN, AND THE REQUIRED RESPONSE TIME
The statute fixes both the substance of a required response and the time within which it must be given, and separately limits how often a business must respond and how detailed the response must be. As to substance, § 1798.83(a) requires the business to provide, free of charge, two categories of information: under paragraph (1), "In writing or by electronic mail, a list of the categories set forth in paragraph (6) of subdivision (e) that correspond to the personal information disclosed by the business to third parties for the third parties' direct marketing purposes during the immediately preceding calendar year," and under paragraph (2), "In writing or by electronic mail, the names and addresses of all of the third parties that received personal information from the business for the third parties' direct marketing purposes during the preceding calendar year and, if the nature of the third parties' business cannot reasonably be determined from the third parties' name, examples of the products or services marketed, if known to the business, sufficient to give the customer a reasonable indication of the nature of the third parties' business." As to timing, § 1798.83(b)(1) sets two different deadlines depending on where the request was received: "The response to a request pursuant to this section received at one of the designated addresses or numbers shall be provided within 30 days. Requests received by the business at other than one of the designated addresses or numbers shall be provided within a reasonable period, in light of the circumstances related to how the request was received, but not to exceed 150 days from the date received." Two further limits apply regardless of content or timing: under § 1798.83(c)(1), "A business that is required to comply with this section is not obligated to do so in response to a request from a customer more than once during the course of any calendar year," and under § 1798.83(b)(3), "A business that is required to comply with this section is not obligated to provide information associated with specific individuals and may provide the information required by this section in standardized format."

THE ALTERNATIVE: A STATED "DO NOT SHARE" OPT-OUT (OR OPT-IN) POLICY
The statute does not require every covered business to respond to individual customer requests at all — it offers a second, alternative compliance path built around a public policy statement rather than a per-request response. Under Civil Code § 1798.83(c)(2), "If a business that is required to comply with this section adopts and discloses to the public, in its privacy policy, a policy of not disclosing personal information of customers to third parties for the third parties' direct marketing purposes unless the customer first affirmatively agrees to that disclosure, or of not disclosing the personal information of customers to third parties for the third parties' direct marketing purposes if the customer has exercised an option that prevents that information from being disclosed to third parties for those purposes, as long as the business maintains and discloses the policies, the business may comply with subdivision (a) by notifying the customer of his or her right to prevent disclosure of personal information, and providing the customer with a cost-free means to exercise that right." This describes two alternative policy forms the statute treats as sufficient — an opt-in policy (no third-party direct-marketing disclosure absent the customer's affirmative agreement) or an opt-out policy (no such disclosure once the customer has exercised an option to prevent it) — either of which, if adopted, disclosed in the business's privacy policy, and actually maintained, lets the business satisfy subdivision (a) by pointing the customer to that right and a cost-free way to exercise it, rather than by compiling and sending the category-and-recipient-list response described elsewhere in this statute.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS: "CUSTOMER" AND "DIRECT MARKETING PURPOSES"
Two of the statute's own defined terms materially narrow who can make a request and what kind of third-party use the statute is even concerned with. Under Civil Code § 1798.83(e)(1), "'Customer' means an individual who is a resident of California who provides personal information to a business during the creation of, or throughout the duration of, an established business relationship if the business relationship is primarily for personal, family, or household purposes" — meaning the statute's request right belongs to California residents in a personal-, family-, or household-purpose relationship with the business, not to every person about whom the business holds data, and not to a business-to-business counterparty. Under § 1798.83(e)(2), "'Direct marketing purposes' means the use of personal information to solicit or induce a purchase, rental, lease, or exchange of products, goods, property, or services directly to individuals by means of the mail, telephone, or electronic mail for their personal, family, or household purposes" — a definition centered on solicitation of individual consumers by mail, telephone, or email, rather than every commercial use a third party might make of shared data.

REMEDIES AVAILABLE FOR A VIOLATION OF SECTION 1798.83
The Customer Records title of the Civil Code — the same title that contains § 1798.83 — sets out several remedies in Civil Code § 1798.84, and several of them are drafted specifically around a § 1798.83 violation rather than only generally. A customer has a general civil action: under § 1798.84(b), "Any customer injured by a violation of this title may institute a civil action to recover damages." On top of that general action, § 1798.84(c) fixes a civil penalty specifically for a § 1798.83 violation: "for a willful, intentional, or reckless violation of Section 1798.83, a customer may recover a civil penalty not to exceed three thousand dollars ($3,000) per violation; otherwise, the customer may recover a civil penalty of up to five hundred dollars ($500) per violation for a violation of Section 1798.83." A prevailing customer-plaintiff can also recover fees: under § 1798.84(g), "A prevailing plaintiff in any action commenced under Section 1798.83 shall also be entitled to recover his or her reasonable attorney's fees and costs." The statute separately gives a business, short of a willful, intentional, or reckless violation, a specific cure opportunity: under § 1798.84(d), a business alleged to have failed to provide required § 1798.83 information, provided inaccurate information, or missed the statutory response deadline "may assert as a complete defense in any action in law or equity that it thereafter provided" the complete or accurate or timely information "to all customers who were provided incomplete or inaccurate information, respectively, within 90 days of the date the business knew" of the failure. Finally, injunctive relief is available under § 1798.84(e): "Any business that violates, proposes to violate, or has violated this title may be enjoined."

Section 1798.83 gives a California customer the right to request information about what personal information a business has disclosed to third parties for the third parties' own direct marketing purposes, and requires a covered business to either respond to such requests or adopt a specified alternative opt-out (or opt-in) policy instead. This is a distinct, older statute from the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA/CPRA) and from the California Online Privacy Protection Act (CalOPPA), addressed in other documents; § 1798.83 became operative January 1, 2005 and was last amended effective January 1, 2006, well before the CCPA (2018/2020) or CalOPPA's current form, and it targets a narrower question — third-party direct-marketing disclosure specifically — rather than a business's general data-collection or data-sale practices. Complying with the CCPA or CalOPPA does not by itself satisfy, and is not required in order to trigger, this separate duty, which has its own conditions, its own required response, and its own alternative compliance path. This sheet is an informational record only. It does not itself determine that Acme, Inc. is a business covered by Civil Code § 1798.83, does not determine that any specific disclosure by Acme, Inc. was made to a third party for the third party's direct marketing purposes, does not determine which of the statute's two compliance paths applies to Acme, Inc. or satisfies either path, and does not respond to, or draft a response to, any actual customer request.

The statute's duty to respond to a customer's request is not owed by every business that handles personal information — it is conditioned on a specific combination of facts about an established customer relationship and a prior disclosure. Under Civil Code § 1798.83(a), the duty attaches "if a business has an established business relationship with a customer and has within the immediately preceding calendar year disclosed personal information that corresponds to any of the categories of personal information set forth in paragraph (6) of subdivision (e) to third parties, and if the business knows or reasonably should know that the third parties used the personal information for the third parties' direct marketing purposes." All three elements — an established business relationship, an actual disclosure of a statutorily listed category of personal information within the preceding calendar year, and the business's actual or constructive knowledge that the recipient used it for the recipient's own direct marketing purposes — are conditions of the trigger language itself, not independent alternative triggers. Separately, the statute carves out businesses below a fixed size, regardless of whether the trigger conditions above are otherwise met: under § 1798.83(c)(1), "A business with fewer than 20 full-time or part-time employees is exempt from the requirements of this section."

expectedJSON.body: The statute specifies both how a customer may submit a request and a business's own corresponding duty to designate where such requests should be sent. As to the customer's request, § 1798.83(a) provides that a covered business's duty runs "after the receipt of a written or electronic mail request, or, if the business chooses to receive requests by toll-free telephone or facsimile numbers, a telephone or facsimile request from the customer" — meaning a customer may always request by mail or email, and may additionally request by toll-free phone or fax only if the business has elected to accept requests through those channels. As to the business's own duty, § 1798.83(b)(1) requires that "A business required to comply with this section shall designate a mailing address, electronic mail address, or, if the business chooses to receive requests by telephone or facsimile, a toll-free telephone or facsimile number, to which customers may deliver requests pursuant to subdivision (a)." The same paragraph goes on to require the business to take at least one of several further steps to make that designated channel known — including notifying customer-facing employees of it, or adding a "Your Privacy Rights" link to the business's website — which this clause does not quote in full.

expectedJSON.body: The statute fixes both the substance of a required response and the time within which it must be given, and separately limits how often a business must respond and how detailed the response must be. As to substance, § 1798.83(a) requires the business to provide, free of charge, two categories of information: under paragraph (1), "In writing or by electronic mail, a list of the categories set forth in paragraph (6) of subdivision (e) that correspond to the personal information disclosed by the business to third parties for the third parties' direct marketing purposes during the immediately preceding calendar year," and under paragraph (2), "In writing or by electronic mail, the names and addresses of all of the third parties that received personal information from the business for the third parties' direct marketing purposes during the preceding calendar year and, if the nature of the third parties' business cannot reasonably be determined from the third parties' name, examples of the products or services marketed, if known to the business, sufficient to give the customer a reasonable indication of the nature of the third parties' business." As to timing, § 1798.83(b)(1) sets two different deadlines depending on where the request was received: "The response to a request pursuant to this section received at one of the designated addresses or numbers shall be provided within 30 days. Requests received by the business at other than one of the designated addresses or numbers shall be provided within a reasonable period, in light of the circumstances related to how the request was received, but not to exceed 150 days from the date received." Two further limits apply regardless of content or timing: under § 1798.83(c)(1), "A business that is required to comply with this section is not obligated to do so in response to a request from a customer more than once during the course of any calendar year," and under § 1798.83(b)(3), "A business that is required to comply with this section is not obligated to provide information associated with specific individuals and may provide the information required by this section in standardized format."

expectedJSON.body: The statute does not require every covered business to respond to individual customer requests at all — it offers a second, alternative compliance path built around a public policy statement rather than a per-request response. Under Civil Code § 1798.83(c)(2), "If a business that is required to comply with this section adopts and discloses to the public, in its privacy policy, a policy of not disclosing personal information of customers to third parties for the third parties' direct marketing purposes unless the customer first affirmatively agrees to that disclosure, or of not disclosing the personal information of customers to third parties for the third parties' direct marketing purposes if the customer has exercised an option that prevents that information from being disclosed to third parties for those purposes, as long as the business maintains and discloses the policies, the business may comply with subdivision (a) by notifying the customer of his or her right to prevent disclosure of personal information, and providing the customer with a cost-free means to exercise that right." This describes two alternative policy forms the statute treats as sufficient — an opt-in policy (no third-party direct-marketing disclosure absent the customer's affirmative agreement) or an opt-out policy (no such disclosure once the customer has exercised an option to prevent it) — either of which, if adopted, disclosed in the business's privacy policy, and actually maintained, lets the business satisfy subdivision (a) by pointing the customer to that right and a cost-free way to exercise it, rather than by compiling and sending the category-and-recipient-list response described elsewhere in this statute.

expectedJSON.body: Two of the statute's own defined terms materially narrow who can make a request and what kind of third-party use the statute is even concerned with. Under Civil Code § 1798.83(e)(1), "'Customer' means an individual who is a resident of California who provides personal information to a business during the creation of, or throughout the duration of, an established business relationship if the business relationship is primarily for personal, family, or household purposes" — meaning the statute's request right belongs to California residents in a personal-, family-, or household-purpose relationship with the business, not to every person about whom the business holds data, and not to a business-to-business counterparty. Under § 1798.83(e)(2), "'Direct marketing purposes' means the use of personal information to solicit or induce a purchase, rental, lease, or exchange of products, goods, property, or services directly to individuals by means of the mail, telephone, or electronic mail for their personal, family, or household purposes" — a definition centered on solicitation of individual consumers by mail, telephone, or email, rather than every commercial use a third party might make of shared data.

expectedJSON.body: The Customer Records title of the Civil Code — the same title that contains § 1798.83 — sets out several remedies in Civil Code § 1798.84, and several of them are drafted specifically around a § 1798.83 violation rather than only generally. A customer has a general civil action: under § 1798.84(b), "Any customer injured by a violation of this title may institute a civil action to recover damages." On top of that general action, § 1798.84(c) fixes a civil penalty specifically for a § 1798.83 violation: "for a willful, intentional, or reckless violation of Section 1798.83, a customer may recover a civil penalty not to exceed three thousand dollars ($3,000) per violation; otherwise, the customer may recover a civil penalty of up to five hundred dollars ($500) per violation for a violation of Section 1798.83." A prevailing customer-plaintiff can also recover fees: under § 1798.84(g), "A prevailing plaintiff in any action commenced under Section 1798.83 shall also be entitled to recover his or her reasonable attorney's fees and costs." The statute separately gives a business, short of a willful, intentional, or reckless violation, a specific cure opportunity: under § 1798.84(d), a business alleged to have failed to provide required § 1798.83 information, provided inaccurate information, or missed the statutory response deadline "may assert as a complete defense in any action in law or equity that it thereafter provided" the complete or accurate or timely information "to all customers who were provided incomplete or inaccurate information, respectively, within 90 days of the date the business knew" of the failure. Finally, injunctive relief is available under § 1798.84(e): "Any business that violates, proposes to violate, or has violated this title may be enjoined."
